topics.title: The Nurse as Collaborator, the Interprofessional Team & Collaborative Practice
topics.summary: Collaboration is two or more people—including the client and family—combining skills, knowledge, and resources toward a shared health goal; the nurse’s job is to know who brings what, work inside their own scope, and pull the right expertise in at the right moment.
objectives: Define collaboration, interprofessional, and interdisciplinary practice and explain how they differ in this course.
Describe the nurse’s collaborative role with clients, peers, other professionals, professional organizations, and legislators (Box 37.2).
Apply the QSEN Teamwork and Collaboration knowledge–skills–attitudes framework (Box 37.1) to bedside behavior.
Match a client’s problem to the interprofessional team member whose scope best addresses it (Table 37.1), including RD vs. nutritionist and PT vs. OT vs. SLP.
Distinguish what the RN may delegate or assign to LPNs and UAP from what stays with the RN (assessment, teaching, evaluation, unstable clients).
Explain how collaboration relates to health policy, healthcare systems, professionalism, quality improvement, and safety.
Summarize the objectives, benefits, and community settings of interprofessional collaborative practice using Clinical Examples A and B.
topics.bigPicture:
No single professional can safely manage a modern hospital stay. A client recovering from a knee replacement needs the surgeon’s plan, the nurse’s 24-hour assessment, the physical therapist’s mobility plan, the case manager’s discharge coordination, the social worker’s help with money and equipment—and, most of all, the client’s and spouse’s own goals. Collaboration is what turns that crowd of experts into one plan instead of six competing ones. When it fails, you get duplicated tests, mixed messages, missed problems, and readmissions. When it works, morbidity, mortality, errors, and length of stay all go down.

The nurse sits at the center of this network because the nurse is the professional who is with the client around the clock, notices change first, and knows which colleague owns which problem. That is why the NCLEX does not just ask you to define collaboration—it hands you a client with a swallowing problem, a stair barrier at home, or an unstable vital sign and asks who should be involved, what the nurse can hand off, and what the nurse must keep.

Think of this topic as learning the “map” of the team: who is on it, what each person’s scope is, where the RN’s accountability begins and ends, and why including the client as a full partner is not just polite—it is the definition of collaborative care.

keyTerms.def: Two or more individuals working together toward a common goal by combining their skills, knowledge, and resources to deliver high-quality care while avoiding duplication of effort (WHO, 2010). Ideally a dynamic process in which clients (individuals, groups, or communities) work with physicians, nurses, and other healthcare providers to meet health objectives; Henderson (1991) called it a partnership among doctors, nurses, other providers, clients, and families.

Professionals from various disciplines (nurses, physicians, pharmacists, therapists) working together; in this module it also includes support staff, the client, and family members—anyone working together for the client’s benefit.
A term often used to signal that paraprofessionals (such as unlicensed assistive personnel or technicians) are included on the team alongside professionals from various disciplines.
Students from two or more professions learning with, from, and about each other so they can work in teams to provide safe, quality care; the NLN calls on nursing schools to build IPE.

One of six QSEN competencies (with patient-centered [client-centered] care, evidence-based practice, quality improvement, safety, and informatics): functioning effectively within nursing and interprofessional teams, fostering open communication, mutual respect, and shared decision making.

Workers not licensed to perform nursing care (CNAs/nurse aides, home health aides, patient care technicians) who carry out delegated activities such as hygiene, feeding, and ambulation; state boards of nursing define RN-to-UAP delegation rules.
Usually a nurse or social worker who coordinates quality care and resources across settings to produce quality, timely, and fiscally sound outcomes.

The RD/RDN is credentialed after a degree, supervised practice, and a national registration exam and provides medical nutrition therapy for acute and chronic disease; a nutritionist may lack formal credentials and teaches general healthy eating but does not provide medical nutrition therapy.

A care model in which multiple professions, the client, and family work interdependently to provide client-centered, continuous, high-quality, cost-effective, evidence-based care across the health continuum.

Delegation transfers the authority to perform a specific task to a competent person while the RN keeps accountability for the outcome; assignment allocates care or clients to staff who are already authorized by their own scope to perform that care.

sections.heading: What collaboration really means (and what it is not)
sections.body:
Collaboration is not the same as “being nice to coworkers,” and it is not the same as following orders. The WHO definition has three working parts: a common goal, combined skills, knowledge, and resources, and avoiding duplication. If the nurse, PT, and case manager each separately teach stair safety and give three different answers, they have worked in parallel—not collaborated. If the physician decides and the nurse silently carries out the plan without contributing assessment data, that is a hierarchy, not a partnership.

Henderson’s phrase “partnership relationship … with patients and their families” is the piece students forget most. The client is a team member with an equal voice. On the NCLEX, an answer that makes decisions for the client and then informs them is almost always weaker than one that involves the client in setting mutually agreed-on goals.

Collaboration happens at three levels: nurse with client, healthcare providers with client, and providers from different professional backgrounds with each other. To function well, nurses need accountability, authority in their practice area, and continuing education in role exploration, communication, and group work.
sections.analogy: A collaborative team is like a pit crew, not a relay race. In a relay, each runner does a leg alone and hands off. In a pit crew, everyone works on the same car at the same moment, each with a distinct job, all watching the same clock—and the driver (the client) tells them where the car is going.

check.q: A physical therapist and a nurse each teach a client a different method for getting out of bed after hip surgery. What collaboration principle is missing?
check.a: A common goal with combined, non-duplicated effort. They should agree on one method in the plan of care and reinforce the same teaching.

sections.heading: Professional standards: QSEN, ANA, NLN and the K-S-A framework
sections.body:
Three professional bodies anchor collaboration as a nursing expectation. QSEN (Quality and Safety Education for Nurses) lists Teamwork and Collaboration as one of six core competencies. The ANA Standards of Professional Nursing Practice include a collaboration standard (Standard 10 in the edition the course cites). The NLN (National League for Nursing) calls on schools to build interprofessional education so students practice teamwork before they graduate.

Box 37.1 breaks the QSEN competency into knowledge (K), skills (S), and attitudes (A). Knowledge is what you understand, skills are what you visibly do, and attitudes are what you value. Exam items usually describe a skill—a behavior—and ask which action shows the competency. Watch for behaviors such as requesting help when needed, clarifying roles, soliciting input, initiating conflict resolution, and following best practices during handoffs.

check.q: A new nurse realizes she has never titrated a heparin infusion and asks the charge nurse to walk through the protocol with her. Which QSEN element does this show?
check.a: Scope and roles skill—functioning within own scope and requesting help when needed (also self-awareness of limitations).

sections.heading: The nurse as collaborator across domains (Box 37.2)
sections.body:
The nurse collaborates in five directions. With clients, the nurse encourages active involvement and autonomy, treats the client as an equal team member, helps set mutually agreed-on goals, and consults in a collaborative fashion. With peers, the nurse shares expertise and draws on others’ expertise, building trust and mutual respect. With other healthcare professionals, the nurse recognizes each member’s expertise, listens to every viewpoint, shares responsibility for exploring options and making care-plan decisions, and joins collaborative research. With professional nursing organizations, the nurse serves on committees and supports political solutions. With legislators, the nurse offers expert opinion on health legislation and works with other providers and consumers to serve public needs.

The client domain is the most heavily tested. The key verbs are involve, encourage, agree on, consult. The wrong-answer verbs are decide for, tell, insist, convince.
sections.example: A client with heart failure says, “I can’t give up salt completely—I eat with my family every Sunday.” A collaborative nurse responds, “Let’s look at what Sunday dinner usually includes and set a sodium goal you think you can stick with; I’ll ask the dietitian to join us.” The goal is mutual, the client’s life is respected, and the right expert is pulled in.

sections.heading: Who is on the team: matching the problem to the professional (Table 37.1)
sections.body:
Many NCLEX items are really “who owns this problem?” questions. Read the client’s problem, translate it into a function (swallowing, ADLs, gait, breathing, money, medication, nutrition), then pick the discipline whose scope matches. The RN coordinates and assesses, but the best answer often involves referring to the right specialist after the nurse’s own assessment.

Two distinctions the course flags as exam traps: only the registered dietitian provides medical nutrition therapy (a renal, cardiac, or diabetic diet plan); a nutritionist teaches general healthy eating. And nurses must check their state Nurse Practice Act and agency policy before carrying out orders written by a physician assistant.

check.q: A client with rheumatoid arthritis cannot button her blouse or open jars. Which referral fits best, and why not PT?
check.a: Occupational therapy—the problem is performing daily activities with the hands and needs adaptive devices. PT focuses on mobility, gait, and musculoskeletal strength and function rather than ADL adaptation.

sections.heading: Scope, delegation, and assignment inside the team
sections.body:
Collaboration does not erase scope of practice—it depends on it. The RN is accountable for assessment, nursing judgment, planning, teaching, and evaluation. The LPN/LVN contributes to care under RN or provider supervision, usually for stable clients with predictable outcomes. UAP perform delegated tasks. A task can be delegated; the nursing process cannot.

Use the five rights of delegation (NCSBN/ANA): right task, right circumstance, right person, right directions and communication, and right supervision and evaluation. Never delegate initial assessment, client teaching, evaluation of a response, or care of an unstable or unpredictable client to UAP. When delegating, give clear, specific directions (“Ambulate Mr. Ruiz 50 feet with the walker at 1000 and 1400; report dizziness or a pulse over 110 to me right away”), then follow up.
steps: Ask: Is the client stable, and is the outcome predictable? If not, keep the client with the RN.
Ask: Does the task require assessment, teaching, evaluation, or nursing judgment? If yes, it stays with the RN.
Ask: Is the task within this person’s legal scope, job description, and agency policy—and has competence been verified?
Give specific directions: what, when, how much, and exactly what to report back.
Supervise and evaluate: check the outcome, receive the report, and reassess the client yourself.

check.q: Which client could the RN delegate to a UAP for routine vital signs: a client 2 hours after a cardiac catheterization with a new irregular pulse, or a client with stable COPD awaiting discharge tomorrow?
check.a: The client with stable COPD. The post-catheterization client with a new irregular pulse is unstable and needs RN assessment.

sections.heading: Collaboration and related concepts; what collaborative practice is for
sections.body:
The course links collaboration to five neighboring concepts, and each link is a cause-and-effect chain you can reason with. Better collaboration raises job satisfaction (health policy), reduces duplicated services and costs (healthcare systems), increases perceived professional autonomy (professionalism), increases situational awareness and teamwork (quality improvement), and lowers morbidity and mortality (safety).

Interprofessional collaborative practice aims to: (1) provide client-directed, client-centered care using a participative framework; (2) enhance continuity across the health continuum from prevention to rehabilitation; (3) improve client and family satisfaction; (4) provide high-quality, cost-effective, evidence-based care; (5) promote mutual respect, communication, and understanding; (6) address and resolve system issues; and (7) develop interdependent relationships among providers and clients.

How to use these links on an exam, step by step. (1) Read what the stem says is improving or getting worse—cost, satisfaction, autonomy, situational awareness, or morbidity and mortality. (2) Ask which concept that outcome belongs to (cost = healthcare systems; job satisfaction = health policy; autonomy = professionalism; situational awareness = quality improvement; morbidity and mortality = safety). (3) Pick the nursing action from that row of the course table—for example, for safety: take part in interprofessional team meetings and raise concerns; for professionalism: teach other team members what nurses do. Evaluation questions run the same chain backward: if collaboration is working, you should see fewer duplicated services, better retention, and fewer complications.

check.q: A hospital’s readmission and duplicate-imaging rates fall a year after it starts interprofessional rounds. Which related concept does this outcome best illustrate, and why?
check.a: Healthcare systems—greater collaboration reduces duplication of services and lowers healthcare costs. (Fewer complications and deaths would illustrate safety; higher nurse satisfaction would illustrate health policy.)

sections.heading: Collaborative practice beyond the hospital and Clinical Examples A & B
sections.body:
Collaboration is just as central outside acute care. Skilled nursing, rehabilitation, and long-term care combine nursing, medical, PT/OT/speech/respiratory therapy, social services, and mental health. Schools serve children with disabilities or medically fragile conditions with nurses, teachers, administrators, counselors, mental health specialists, PT, OT, SLP, and physicians. Assertive Community Treatment (ACT) supports people with serious mental illness (such as schizophrenia or bipolar disorder) at home and in the community through psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, pharmacists, APRNs, employment counselors, and peer support specialists. PACE (Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly) helps older adults stay in the community with medical care, respite, transportation, and mental health services.

Clinical Example A (Mr. Hainsley) wants to go home after a knee replacement despite stairs. The primary nurse, RN case manager, PT, social worker, and surgical resident meet with him and his spouse; they respect his goal, arrange home health and PT home-safety assessments, solve money and equipment barriers through social work, and document the shared decision. Clinical Example B (Mr. Eliot) has heart failure, chronic renal failure, hypertension, and BPH. Daily interprofessional rounds with nurse, physician, dietitian, and case manager address fluid volume excess, urinary retention, impaired gas exchange, and anxiety; the diuretic is lowered once he is stable, the dietitian teaches a low-sodium diet, and home care is arranged—preventing complications and easing anxiety.
sections.example: Apply the pattern: a client in the ACT program misses two depot injections and stops attending appointments. The community nurse does not act alone—she contacts the ACT team so the psychiatrist, social worker, and peer support specialist can coordinate outreach, assess housing or transportation barriers, and revise the plan with the client.

check.q: A 34-year-old with schizophrenia keeps missing clinic visits and was hospitalized twice this year after stopping medication. An 82-year-old with diabetes and arthritis wants to stay home but her caregiver needs relief and she has no transportation. Which community program fits each?
check.a: The 34-year-old fits Assertive Community Treatment (ACT)—a community mental health team for serious mental illness. The 82-year-old fits PACE—all-inclusive community care for older adults with medical care, respite, transportation, and mental health services.
