sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: choosing the right team member and the right handoff
sections.body:
Expect three patterns. Referral items give a client problem and four disciplines. Delegation and assignment items list clients or tasks and ask which can go to the LPN or UAP. Collaboration-behavior items ask which nurse action best demonstrates collaboration with the client or team, or which statement by a new nurse needs further teaching. The winning answer respects scope, involves the client, and avoids duplication.

Sample question: A client 3 days after a stroke coughs and clears his throat each time he drinks water, and his voice sounds wet. His daughter asks for thin liquids because “he hates thickened drinks.” Which action should the nurse take first? A. Ask the dietitian to calculate fluid needs. B. Hold oral fluids and request a swallowing evaluation by the speech-language pathologist. C. Teach the daughter to give small sips through a straw. D. Ask the UAP to stay with the client during meals.
steps: Read the stem: coughing and a wet voice with water after a stroke = cues of aspiration risk (dysphagia).
Identify what is asked: the FIRST action—so safety (airway) outranks preference and comfort.
Spot the cue that points to a discipline: swallowing problems belong to the speech-language pathologist.

Eliminate A: fluid calculation matters later, but it does not address aspiration risk. Eliminate C: straws can increase aspiration risk, and teaching a technique before evaluation is unsafe. Eliminate D: UAP supervision does not fix unsafe swallowing and delegates a client who needs assessment.

Choose B: protect the airway by holding oral intake and get the expert evaluation; then address the daughter’s concern collaboratively once the SLP recommends a safe texture. Note: if one option had been “assess the client’s respiratory status,” that would come before the referral—the nurse’s own assessment and safety action always precede bringing in the specialist (compare the practice question on the client who sounds “gurgly” after juice).
Reusable strategy: translate the problem into a body function, match the function to the discipline, and pick the option that keeps the client safe while involving that expert.

sections.heading: Worked case: discharge planning with a reluctant team
sections.body:
Mrs. Alvarez, 78, is ready for discharge after hip fracture repair. She lives alone in a second-floor apartment, uses a walker, takes 11 medications, and tells you, “I am not going to a nursing home. My cat needs me.” The surgeon’s note says “discharge to rehab facility.” Her son lives an hour away and worries she will fall. The unit is busy, and a colleague says, “Just tell her the doctor decided.”

Collaboration here means building one plan with Mrs. Alvarez at the center, using each discipline’s expertise, rather than overriding her or ignoring safety.
steps: Recognize cues: fall risk (walker, stairs, lives alone), polypharmacy (11 medications), strong client preference, family concern, and a plan written without the client’s input.
Clarify the client’s goal: ask what matters most and what she would accept (home with help, short rehab stay, home health). Her autonomy is a starting point, not an obstacle.

Bring in the right disciplines: PT for stair and transfer safety, OT for bathing and kitchen safety, pharmacist for medication reconciliation, case manager for home health or short-term rehab options, social worker for cost and caregiver resources.
Request an interprofessional care conference that includes Mrs. Alvarez and, with her permission, her son, so options are discussed together rather than delivered as a decision.
Document the shared plan, who owns each action, and the follow-up (for example, home safety evaluation within 48 hours).
Evaluate: Can she demonstrate safe stair technique? Can she state her medication schedule? Is the home equipment delivered? Revise if not.

check.q: Why is “Just tell her the doctor decided” the wrong collaborative response even though rehab might ultimately be the safest choice?
check.a: It removes the client from the team and replaces shared decision making with status-based authority. The team may still recommend rehab, but the recommendation should come from joint assessment and discussion with the client, who keeps the right to decide.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
In North Carolina, nursing is regulated by the North Carolina Board of Nursing (NCBON) under the Nursing Practice Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. Chapter 90, Article 9A, G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.). The RN and LPN components of practice are in 21 NCAC 36 .0224 (RN) and .0225 (LPN). The RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment; the LPN participates under RN or provider supervision; the RN may delegate tasks, not the nursing process or nursing judgment.

North Carolina has two aide levels. The Nurse Aide I registry is kept by NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation. The Nurse Aide II registry is kept by NCBON, and an NA II must also be on the NA I registry; NA II tasks include some more advanced tasks (for example, sterile dressing changes and oxygen-related tasks) per the NCBON NA II task list. A task must be on the aide’s approved list and the RN must decide that delegation is appropriate for that specific client at that time. NCBON publishes a “Decision Tree for Delegation to UAP” and a scope-of-practice decision tree that you can use when unsure.

North Carolina is a Nurse Licensure Compact state, so a multistate license allows practice across compact states—but you always practice under the nurse practice act of the state where the client is located. The course’s PA reminder applies here too: confirm what your state’s rules and agency policy allow before implementing an order written by a physician assistant.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body:
Source: Module 37 study guide, pp. 2553–2556 (definitions, QSEN/ANA/NLN, Box 37.1, Box 37.2, Table 37.1, related concepts) and pp. 2558–2559 (interprofessional collaborative practice, benefits, community settings, Clinical Examples A and B).

Clarifications: (1) The source lists the “National League for Nurses”; the organization’s correct name is the National League for Nursing. (2) The source cites ANA Standard 10 for collaboration; that numbering comes from the 2015 edition—the 2021 (4th) edition renumbered the standards and collaboration appears as Standard 11. The expectation is the same. (3) The source calls the RD “board-certified to diagnose/treat medical nutrition therapy.” More precisely, RDs/RDNs are credentialed by the Commission on Dietetic Registration and provide medical nutrition therapy and nutrition diagnoses; they do not make medical diagnoses. (4) Many references use “interprofessional” and “interdisciplinary” loosely; learn the course’s distinction for exams, but focus clinically on who is on the team and what they do. (5) The five rights of delegation and the rule against delegating assessment, teaching, evaluation, or unstable clients are standard NCSBN/ANA principles added because they belong to the team-roles content.

mnemonics.name: 5 Rights of Delegation
mnemonics.text: Task, Circumstance, Person, Directions/Communication, Supervision/Evaluation—“The Careful Person Directs and Supervises.”

mnemonics.name: Who owns the function?
mnemonics.text: PT = Paths (walking, stairs); OT = Occupations (dressing, cooking, ADLs); SLP = Swallow & Speech; RD = Recipes for disease (medical nutrition therapy); SW = Support & Safety-net (money, coping, protection).

pearls: The client is a full member of the team—answers that involve the client in setting goals beat answers that inform the client of decisions.
Collaboration requires a common goal and no duplication; three disciplines teaching three different methods is a collaboration failure.
Coughing or a wet voice with fluids = hold oral intake and involve the SLP before any diet change.
Disease-specific diets go to the registered dietitian, not a nutritionist.
Check the state Nurse Practice Act and agency policy before implementing PA orders.
Delegate tasks, never the nursing process: assessment, teaching, evaluation, and unstable clients stay with the RN.
Case manager coordinates services across settings; social worker tackles coping, money, and protection.
redFlags: A care plan written without the client’s input, especially one the client has rejected—stop and bring the client into the decision.
A UAP assigned to a client whose condition is changing or unpredictable.
Signs of aspiration (coughing, wet voice, desaturation with meals) while the client continues to receive thin liquids.
Conflicting instructions from different disciplines that the client cannot reconcile—call a team conference.
An order from an unfamiliar prescriber type you are unsure you may implement—verify before acting.
recap: Collaboration = common goal + combined skills/knowledge/resources + no duplication, with the client as a partner.
QSEN Teamwork and Collaboration is one of six competencies; Box 37.1 breaks it into knowledge, skills, and attitudes.
The nurse collaborates with clients, peers, other professionals, professional organizations, and legislators.
Match the client’s problem to the discipline whose scope fits (PT mobility, OT ADLs, SLP swallowing, RD medical nutrition therapy, SW psychosocial/financial, case manager coordination).
The RN keeps assessment, teaching, evaluation, and unstable clients; use the five rights to delegate tasks.
Collaboration improves outcomes for clients (morbidity, mortality, errors, LOS), teams (satisfaction, retention), and systems (cost, coordination, access).
Community models include SNF/rehab/LTC, schools, ACT for serious mental illness, and PACE for older adults.
Clinical Examples A and B show discharge planning and daily rounds that respect client goals and divide work by expertise.

checks.q: A client with new-onset type 1 diabetes and celiac disease asks the nurse for a meal plan. A wellness nutritionist is available today; the RD is available tomorrow. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Refer to the registered dietitian for medical nutrition therapy; reinforce general information meanwhile. A nutritionist does not provide disease-specific medical nutrition therapy.

checks.q: Which is the better collaborative statement: “The team has decided you will go to rehab” or “The team recommends rehab—tell us what concerns you about that so we can look at options together”? Why?
checks.a: The second. It keeps the client as a partner with autonomy in the decision; the first is status-based and excludes the client.

checks.q: An RN has a UAP and four clients. One has a new oxygen saturation of 88% and new confusion. Which tasks for this client can the UAP perform?
checks.a: Only supportive tasks the RN directs after RN assessment (for example, staying with the client or repositioning as instructed). The RN must assess, intervene, and evaluate; the client is unstable.

checks.q: A school nurse is planning for a child with a tracheostomy and spastic cerebral palsy. Name three team members and the specific contribution of each.
checks.a: Examples: RT or school nurse for airway care plan; PT for mobility and positioning; OT for classroom adaptive devices; SLP for communication and feeding; teacher and administrator for classroom accommodations; physician for orders.

checks.q: During daily rounds, the dietitian, physician, nurse, and case manager each review a client with heart failure. Which data would show the collaborative plan is working?
checks.a: Daily weight trending down toward dry weight, clearer lung sounds, improved oxygenation, client correctly describing low-sodium choices, and a home care plan in place—with reduced anxiety.

checks.q: A colleague says, “Collaboration just means I follow the provider’s orders carefully.” How would you correct this?
checks.a: Collaboration is a partnership: the nurse contributes assessment data, nursing judgment, and the client’s perspective to shared decision making, speaks up about concerns, and works toward a common goal—not just carrying out orders.

topics.title: IPEC Core Competencies & TeamSTEPPS Communication
topics.summary: The four IPEC competencies—values/ethics, roles/responsibilities, communication, and teams/teamwork—describe how a team actually works, and TeamSTEPPS tools (SBAR, call-out, checkback, CUS, Two-Challenge Rule, I PASS THE BATON) turn those competencies into safe, standardized communication.
objectives: Explain the four IPEC core competencies and identify behaviors that demonstrate each one.
Describe how mutual respect and trust develop and why they cannot be assumed.
Contrast status-based and team-centered communication and rewrite a status-based statement in team-centered form.
Organize a provider call or handoff using SBAR and I PASS THE BATON.
Use call-out, checkback, CUS, and the Two-Challenge Rule correctly, including when to escalate up the chain of command.
Identify barriers to nurse–physician collaboration and select evidence-based strategies to overcome them.
Include clients and families as team members in rounds and decision making.
topics.bigPicture:
Communication failures among providers are a major cause of adverse events. Most serious errors are not caused by someone who did not know the right drug or dose—they happen because the person who noticed the problem did not say it clearly, said it to the wrong person, was not heard, or did not push hard enough. A nurse who sees a client’s pressure dropping and says, “Um, he looks kind of off,” has assessed well and communicated poorly.

The IPEC competencies describe the foundation (respect, knowing roles, communicating, working as a team), and TeamSTEPPS—developed by the Department of Defense and AHRQ—gives you scripts so that critical information comes out in a predictable shape even under stress. Scripts flatten hierarchy: a new graduate using CUS (“I am concerned… I am uncomfortable… this is a safety issue”) carries the same weight as a 20-year veteran because the words are recognized team signals.

On the NCLEX, this topic shows up as “which statement by the nurse is best,” “what should the nurse include,” “which technique is the nurse using,” and “what should the nurse do next after the provider dismisses the concern.” The right answer is almost always the one that is clear, specific, closed-loop, and escalates when safety is still at risk.

keyTerms.def: Four domains identified by the Interprofessional Education Collaborative essential to improving outcomes and quality: values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, interprofessional communication, and teams and teamwork.
Team members value the contributions and knowledge of each member and treat all members as equals, acknowledging the uniqueness and differing views each person and profession brings.
Confidence a team member has in the actions of another individual; like mutual respect, it is a shared process nurtured and developed over time, not automatic.
Hierarchical, intimidating, one-sided communication (“Give this,” “You need to do X”) that discourages others from speaking up and increases error risk.

Communication that flattens hierarchy, shows appreciation, and focuses on “we” (“Mr. X is concerned about… What are your thoughts?”), using attentive listening, acknowledging other perspectives, stating one’s own view, and give-and-take.
An evidence-based teamwork system developed by the Department of Defense and AHRQ to reduce errors, flatten hierarchies, and standardize communication during routine care and risky handoffs.
Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation/Request—a structured tool for communicating critical client information, especially in provider calls and handoffs.

The transfer and acceptance of client-care responsibility from one nurse or provider to another, such as at shift change or care transitions; standardized tools are used because transitions carry high safety risk.
Reporting critical information to all team members at the same time during urgent or emergent events so everyone hears it and anticipates next steps (“Blood pressure?” “86/60”).
Closed-loop communication in which the receiver repeats back critical information and the sender confirms it is correct (order → repeat back → “That’s correct”).
An escalation script for safety concerns: “I am Concerned… I am Uncomfortable… This is a Safety issue.”

Gives every team member the right and duty to voice a safety concern at least twice to make sure it is heard; the challenged person must acknowledge it, and if the concern is still unaddressed the member takes stronger action and goes up the chain of command.
A structured handoff tool: Introduction, Patient, Assessment, Situation, Safety concerns, THE (a connecting word, not a step), Background, Actions, Timing, Ownership, Next.
A common understanding among team members of the plan, the roles, and the client’s status, built through huddles, briefings, and interdisciplinary rounds.

sections.heading: The four IPEC competencies at a glance
sections.body: IPEC (2016) names four core competencies. They build on each other: you cannot communicate well with someone you do not respect, and you cannot use people’s skills if you do not know their roles. Exam items often describe a behavior and ask which competency it demonstrates, so learn each by what it looks like.

rows: Work with others and the client in a mutually respectful way that builds trust and shared goals of quality and safety
Honoring the client’s and team’s diversity, values, and preferences; treating each member as an equal
Dismissing the UAP’s observation because “she’s just an aide”
Understand and appreciate every member’s role and scope; use each person’s unique skills
Explaining each member’s role to the client; calling the pharmacist for an interaction question; continuing education
Nurse attempting to adjust ventilator settings that belong to RT protocol without consulting
Communication is the basic method of collaboration and essential to safety
SBAR calls, closed-loop checkback, team-centered language
Vague, status-based, or one-way communication; skipped repeat-back
Team goals come before individual goals; client and family are members
Discipline-specific input followed by discussion and shared decisions; family invited to rounds
Each discipline acting alone; family excluded from rounds

check.q: A nurse explains to a client, “The respiratory therapist will manage your breathing treatments, and the pharmacist will review all your home medicines with you before discharge.” Which competency is this?
check.a: Roles and responsibilities—clearly communicating each member’s role to the client and using each person’s unique skills.

sections.heading: Values, ethics, and roles: respect and trust are built, not assumed
sections.body:
Mutual respect means valuing every member’s knowledge and treating everyone as equals, including the client and paraprofessionals. Trust means being confident in another person’s actions. The course stresses that neither happens automatically—historical healthcare culture did not always promote interprofessional respect, so teams must build it on purpose: following through on what you say you will do, acknowledging good catches, admitting your own limits, and listening to people outside your profession.

Roles and responsibilities require each member to understand and appreciate the scope of everyone else. That is what lets the nurse say, “This is a question for the pharmacist,” instead of guessing, and what lets the team divide work without duplication. Each member also takes responsibility for continuing education and professional development and communicates their role clearly to the client so the client knows whom to ask about what.
sections.example: A UAP tells the nurse, “Mrs. Park didn’t want breakfast and seems sleepier than yesterday.” A respectful, trust-building response is, “Thank you—that’s an important change. I’ll go assess her now.” The nurse then tells the UAP what was found. The aide learns that speaking up is valued, which increases the chance she will report the next change too.

sections.heading: Communication styles: concise vs. descriptive, status-based vs. team-centered
sections.body:
Physicians are typically trained to communicate concisely, while nurses tend to use a more descriptive, narrative style. Neither is wrong, but the mismatch causes friction: a long story at 0300 may lose the listener before the key request is made. One study of pediatric ICU family meetings found physicians spoke about 90% of the time—another reminder that the client’s and family’s voices can get crowded out.

The bigger safety issue is status-based versus team-centered communication. Status-based communication is one-sided and hierarchical; it signals “do not question me,” so people stay silent and errors slip through. Team-centered communication uses “we,” invites input, acknowledges other perspectives, and states one’s own view honestly.

rows: “You need to get him up now.”
“We want him walking before lunch—what’s a good time for you to get him up?”
“His pain is 8/10 and respirations are 12—what are your thoughts on dosing?”
Brings data and invites shared judgment
“Thanks for flagging that—let’s check the protocol together.”
Keeps people willing to speak up
“Mr. X is worried about going to rehab. How can we address that?”
Puts the client’s concern at the center

check.q: Rewrite in team-centered form: “You need to call the family and tell them visiting hours are over.”
check.a: Example: “Our client seems exhausted—could we talk with the family together about a visiting plan that lets him rest?”

sections.heading: SBAR: making a provider call that gets results
sections.body: SBAR is the standard shape for critical information. It fixes the concise-versus-descriptive mismatch by putting the situation first and ending with a clear request. Before you call: assess the client yourself, review recent vital signs, labs, medications, allergies, and the code status, and have the chart in front of you. The Recommendation is where students most often fall short—a call that ends without a request leaves the provider guessing what you need.
steps: Situation: who you are, who the client is, and what is happening right now. “This is Jen, RN on 4 West, calling about Mr. Lee in 412. His oxygen saturation dropped to 87% on 2 L.”
Background: relevant context. “He is post-op day 2 from a bowel resection, has COPD, and received hydromorphone 1 mg IV 40 minutes ago.”
Assessment: your data and your interpretation. “Respirations 10 and shallow, he is difficult to arouse, lungs diminished in the bases. I am concerned about opioid-related respiratory depression.”
Recommendation/Request: what you need. “I’d like an order for naloxone and for you to evaluate him now. Should we increase his oxygen while you come?”
Close the loop: read back any orders received and document the call, the response, and the time.

check.q: A nurse calls a provider: “Mrs. Diaz, 68, admitted with pneumonia, has a temperature of 39.4°C, HR 118, BP 92/54, and new confusion; I think she may be developing sepsis.” What is missing?
check.a: The Recommendation/Request—for example, asking the provider to evaluate the client now and requesting orders for blood cultures, lactate, and fluids per the sepsis protocol.

sections.heading: Call-out, checkback, and handoff with I PASS THE BATON
sections.body:
During emergencies, information must reach everyone at once. A call-out broadcasts a critical value to the whole team (“Blood pressure?” “86 over 60!”) so the physician, the RT, and the nurse drawing up medications all anticipate the next step together. A checkback closes the loop on a specific message: the receiver repeats it, and the sender confirms. Use checkback for every verbal or telephone order, critical lab value, and medication instruction—not only when you are unsure.

A handoff is a high-risk moment because responsibility changes hands; QSEN asks nurses to acknowledge that care transitions are risky and to use best practices to minimize risk. I PASS THE BATON gives handoffs a standard order so nothing critical is skipped—especially the Safety section.

table.caption: I PASS THE BATON
rows: “I’m Sam, the RN going off; this is Ms. Grant.”
Assessment—chief complaint, symptoms, diagnosis, vital signs
Situation—current status, recent changes, response to treatment
Insulin drip at 4 units/h, glucose trending down
Safety concerns—critical labs, allergies, falls, infection, social issues
K+ 3.2, penicillin allergy, fall risk, contact precautions
“THE” is just a connecting word; B = Background—comorbidities, history, medications
Actions—interventions done or needed, with rationale
Repeat BMP at 1600 because of potassium
Timing—urgency and timing of actions; priorities
Oncoming nurse owns the 1600 lab follow-up
Next—what happens next; anticipated changes; contingency
Transition to subcutaneous insulin when gap closes

sections.analogy: A checkback is like reading your order back at a drive-through window: “One large coffee, no sugar?” “Correct.” It feels redundant until the day it catches “no sugar” being heard as “two sugars.” A call-out is the stadium announcer—everyone hears the score at the same moment.

sections.heading: Speaking up: CUS, the Two-Challenge Rule, and the chain of command
sections.body:
Knowing something is wrong is only half the job; the client is protected only if the concern changes what happens. CUS gives escalating words that the whole team recognizes as a stop signal. The Two-Challenge Rule says you have the right and the duty to voice a safety concern at least twice. The person challenged must acknowledge it. If the concern is still not addressed and the client remains at risk, you take stronger action—typically stopping the activity if possible and going up the chain of command (charge nurse, then nursing supervisor or house manager, then the medical chief or department chair, according to policy).

NCLEX loves the “provider dismissed my concern” stem. Silence, documenting only, or carrying out an unsafe order are wrong. Going straight to the hospital CEO or the state board is also wrong as a first step. The answer is the next level up the chain while keeping the client safe.
steps: First challenge: state the concern clearly with data. “Dr. Shah, the client’s potassium is 6.2 and this order adds potassium chloride.”
If dismissed, use CUS: “I am concerned about hyperkalemia. I am uncomfortable giving this. This is a safety issue.”
Second challenge: repeat the concern and request acknowledgment. The challenged person must respond.
If still unresolved, do not carry out the unsafe action; notify the charge nurse or nursing supervisor and follow the chain of command per policy.
Keep the client safe while escalating (monitor, hold the medication), and document facts objectively per policy.

check.q: A surgeon says “we don’t have time” after a nurse twice states that the consent form lists the left knee but the right knee is prepped. What should the nurse do?
check.a: Stop the procedure from proceeding (call a time-out) and escalate immediately to the charge nurse or perioperative supervisor per the chain of command; do not proceed with a possible wrong-site procedure.

sections.heading: Teams and teamwork; barriers and evidence-based fixes
sections.body:
In true teamwork, members put team goals ahead of individual goals. Clients and families are team members with chances to voice concerns, ask questions, access information, and participate in care. When a discipline-specific concern comes up, the member from that discipline gives expert input, followed by discussion and shared decision making—so the pharmacist leads on the drug interaction, but the decision is the team’s with the client.

Evidence shows nurses and physicians often perceive their collaboration differently: physicians tend to rate communication as more effective than nurses do. Barriers include power struggles, hierarchy, different perceptions of roles and trust, and segregated professional education. Evidence-based solutions attack those root causes.

rows: Team-centered communication; TeamSTEPPS; administrative support for a speak-up culture
Mutual understanding of team roles; interdisciplinary rounding
Join and contribute assessment data at rounds
Participate in IPE and joint drills
Respecting team members; follow-through; shared mental models via huddles and briefings
Close the loop and report back on tasks
Checkback every verbal order; I PASS THE BATON

check.q: At rounds, the pharmacist raises a possible interaction between a client’s new antibiotic and warfarin. According to the Teams and Teamwork competency, how should the decision be made?
check.a: The pharmacist gives discipline-specific input (the interaction and options), then the team—including the client—discusses it and makes a shared decision. The pharmacist leads on the expertise, but the plan belongs to the team and client.

sections.heading: Common traps & look-alikes

rows: Call-out broadcasts to the whole team at once; checkback is a closed loop between sender and receiver
“Announces to the team” vs. “repeats back and sender confirms”
Checkback requires the sender to confirm; repeating with no confirmation is not a closed loop
CUS is the wording; Two-Challenge is the rule to voice it at least twice and then escalate
SBAR vs. I PASS THE BATON
SBAR is compact, ideal for a provider call or concise handoff; I PASS THE BATON is a fuller handoff structure with ownership and next steps
Phone call to provider vs. shift handoff
Situation = what is happening now; Assessment = your data and what you think the problem is
Values/ethics = respect, trust, honoring diversity; roles = knowing and using scope
Chain of command goes one level up at a time; jumping to administration or regulators first is not appropriate
Next appropriate level is usually charge nurse or supervisor

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: communication tools and speaking up
sections.body:
Typical items: identify which tool or technique the nurse is using; choose the best SBAR component or the best way to complete a handoff; select which handoff detail needs follow-up first; and decide what to do when a concern is dismissed. The best option is specific, data-based, closed-loop, and protects the client; vague, silent, or bypassing options lose.

Sample question: During a rapid response, the physician says, “Give amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes.” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate? A. “Okay, I’ll get it right away.” B. “Amiodarone 150 milligrams IV over 10 minutes?” and waits for confirmation. C. Announces to the room, “Heart rate is 168!” D. “I’ll write it down and have you sign it after the code.”
steps: Read the stem: a verbal medication order during an emergency—high error risk, noisy room.
Identify what is asked: the most appropriate response to a verbal order.
Spot cues: a specific drug, dose, route, and rate—exactly the kind of message checkback is designed for.

Eliminate A: acknowledges but does not verify the details. Eliminate C: that is a call-out of a vital sign, useful but not a response to the order. Eliminate D: documentation follows, but the order must be verified before giving it.
Choose B: closed-loop checkback—repeat the exact order and wait for the sender’s confirmation before giving it.

Reusable strategy: match the tool to the message—team-wide critical value = call-out; specific order or value to one person = checkback; unresolved safety concern = CUS then Two-Challenge then chain of command.

sections.heading: Worked case: the concern nobody wanted to hear
sections.body: At 0230, you are caring for Mr. Owens, 64, post-op day 1 from a colectomy. His HR has risen from 88 to 122, BP from 132/80 to 98/58, urine output was 15 mL/h for 2 hours, and he says, “Something feels wrong.” You page the on-call resident, who answers sleepily, “He’s probably just in pain—give his PRN and call me in the morning.” A coworker shrugs: “That resident hates getting called.”
steps: Recognize cues: rising HR, falling BP, low urine output, and the client’s sense of doom—possible hemorrhage or sepsis, not simple pain.
Prepare before (or while) re-calling: reassess the client, check the dressing and drains, review the last hemoglobin, and gather the data in SBAR order.
Use SBAR with a clear request: “I am requesting that you come evaluate him now and order a CBC and lactate.”
When dismissed, use CUS and the Two-Challenge Rule: “I am concerned he is bleeding. I am uncomfortable waiting until morning. This is a safety issue.” Ask for acknowledgment.
If still unresolved, escalate up the chain: charge nurse and nursing supervisor, who can contact the attending; activate the rapid response team if criteria are met—do not wait.
Keep the client safe: monitor frequently, keep IV access, and prepare for interventions.
Document objectively: times, data, people notified, exact responses, and actions taken.

check.q: Your coworker says activating a rapid response will “make the resident look bad.” How do you respond using IPEC values?
check.a: The team’s shared goal is client safety, which comes before individual reputations. Activating the rapid response is a system tool designed for exactly this situation and supports, rather than attacks, the team.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
Under the NC Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.) and the RN component rules (21 NCAC 36 .0224), the RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment. That accountability includes communicating findings to the right person and following through: documenting that you “notified the provider” does not end your duty if the client remains unsafe. Using the chain of command is how an NC nurse meets that accountability.

The NCBON reviews practice events using a Just Culture–based Complaint Evaluation Tool that distinguishes human error (an inadvertent slip), at-risk behavior (a drift such as skipping a read-back because “everyone does”), and reckless behavior (conscious disregard of a substantial, unjustifiable risk). In the general Just Culture model, human error is met by consoling the nurse and fixing the system, at-risk behavior by coaching, and reckless behavior by disciplinary action. This framework rewards honest reporting and system fixes—another reason to use checkback and standardized handoffs consistently. Conduct issues such as drug diversion, impairment on duty, fraud, boundary violations, and confidentiality breaches are reported to the Board rather than handled only by the employer.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body:
Source: Module 37 study guide, pp. 2556–2558 (IPEC competencies, mutual respect and trust, communication styles, status-based vs. team-centered communication, TeamSTEPPS tools, I PASS THE BATON, teams and teamwork, EBP barriers and solutions).

Clarifications: (1) IPEC updated its competencies in 2023 (Version 3); the same four domains—values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, teams and teamwork—remain. (2) TeamSTEPPS 3.0 (AHRQ, 2023) keeps SBAR, call-out, checkback, CUS, the Two-Challenge Rule, and handoff tools; content here matches current versions. (3) The “Safety” step of I PASS THE BATON is labeled “Safety concerns” in TeamSTEPPS materials, and the source’s “THE — Background” line means the word “THE” links the first half of the mnemonic to the B (Background) of BATON; it is not a separate step. (4) Chain-of-command sequence and rapid response activation were added because they are the expected next steps after the Two-Challenge Rule in NCLEX items. (5) The 89.9% physician speaking-time figure comes from a single pediatric ICU study and illustrates a trend rather than a universal rule.

mnemonics.name: CUS
mnemonics.text: Concerned → Uncomfortable → Safety issue: three escalating steps that tell the team to stop and listen.

mnemonics.name: Match the tool to the message
mnemonics.text: Everyone needs it now = Call-out; one person needs it exact = Checkback; it’s still unsafe = CUS → twice → chain of command; changing hands = SBAR or I PASS THE BATON.

pearls: Assess the client and gather data before calling the provider; end every SBAR with a specific request.
Checkback is complete only when the sender confirms the repeat-back.
Use checkback for all verbal and telephone orders and critical values, not just unfamiliar ones.
After voicing a safety concern twice without resolution, escalate up the chain of command—do not proceed and do not stay silent.
Team-centered language (“we,” “what are your thoughts?”) increases speaking up and reduces errors.
Clients and families are team members: invite them to rounds, ask their goals, and answer their questions.
Handoffs are high-risk: give safety concerns (critical labs, allergies, falls, infection) and assign ownership of pending actions.
redFlags: A verbal order acted on without repeat-back and confirmation.
A safety concern dismissed by a team member while the client’s condition is deteriorating.
A handoff with no mention of pending critical labs, allergies, or isolation status.
A unit culture where staff say “that provider hates getting called”—a barrier to speaking up that endangers clients.
Status-based commands that leave a UAP or new nurse afraid to report a change.
recap: IPEC’s four competencies: values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, teams and teamwork.
Mutual respect and trust are built over time through follow-through, listening, and valuing every member.
Team-centered communication flattens hierarchy; status-based communication silences people and increases errors.
SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation/Request—assess first and always make a request.
Call-out = whole team hears a critical value at once; checkback = repeat back and sender confirms.
CUS plus the Two-Challenge Rule: voice the concern at least twice, require acknowledgment, then escalate up the chain.
I PASS THE BATON structures handoffs, including safety concerns, ownership, and next steps.
Barriers (hierarchy, role confusion, segregated education) are reduced by IPE, interdisciplinary rounds, shared mental models, and administrative support.

checks.q: During a code, the nurse says loudly, “Potassium is 7.1!” Which TeamSTEPPS technique is this, and why is it used?
checks.a: A call-out—it broadcasts critical information to the entire team simultaneously so everyone anticipates the next interventions.

checks.q: A provider gives a phone order: “Furosemide 40 mg IV now.” The nurse repeats, “Furosemide 40 mg IV now,” and hangs up. What step is missing?
checks.a: The sender’s confirmation. Checkback is closed-loop: the provider must confirm (“That’s correct”) before the nurse acts.

checks.q: Which SBAR element is “I think he is fluid-overloaded”?
checks.a: Assessment—the nurse’s interpretation of the data. Situation would describe what is happening now; Recommendation is the request.

checks.q: During handoff you learn a client has a potassium of 2.9 drawn 2 hours ago that no one has reported. What does I PASS THE BATON say about this, and what do you do?
checks.a: It belongs under Safety concerns and Ownership. Clarify who owns the follow-up, then assess the client and notify the provider promptly—do not let the finding fall between shifts.

checks.q: A nurse twice tells an anesthesiologist that the client’s allergy band says latex and latex gloves are open on the field. The anesthesiologist ignores her. What next?
checks.a: Stop the exposure if possible and escalate immediately to the charge nurse or supervisor per chain of command, keeping the client safe.

checks.q: A nurse manager wants physicians and nurses to share a mental model of each client’s daily plan. Which strategy is most evidence-based?
checks.a: Interdisciplinary bedside rounds (with client and family) or structured huddles, supported by administration—rather than separate discipline meetings.

topics.title: Conflict Prevention, Conflict Management & Workplace Incivility
topics.summary: Conflict is a normal, unavoidable part of healthcare work; the nurse’s job is to recognize its level and visibility early, prevent what can be prevented, choose the conflict style that fits the situation, and refuse to tolerate incivility and bullying because they endanger clients.
objectives: Define conflict and classify a scenario as intrapersonal, interpersonal, intergroup, or interorganizational.
Distinguish overt from covert conflict using behavioral cues.
Identify individual, interpersonal, organizational, and relationship-specific causes of conflict in healthcare.
Apply staff-level and leadership-level strategies that prevent conflict and reduce stress.
Select the most appropriate Thomas–Kilmann conflict style for a given situation and explain when each is risky.
Apply evidence-based guidelines to manage conflict with colleagues, clients, and families.
Describe incivility, verbal abuse, horizontal violence, and workplace bullying and their effects on team communication and client safety.
topics.bigPicture:
Put a dozen people with different training, goals, workloads, and personalities on a 12-hour shift with sick, frightened clients, and disagreement is guaranteed. The course is blunt about this: conflict can never be completely eliminated. The goal is not a unit where nobody ever disagrees—that unit usually has covert conflict (gossip, absenteeism, quiet sabotage) simmering underneath. The goal is a unit where disagreement is surfaced early and handled constructively, so it becomes an engine for better care instead of a threat to it.

Why does this matter at the bedside? Unmanaged conflict blocks communication, and blocked communication harms clients. A new nurse who is belittled every time she asks a question stops asking. A family that feels ignored escalates to shouting, and the nurse avoids the room. A turf war between two departments delays a test. Every one of those is a safety problem wearing a relationship costume.

On the NCLEX, conflict questions ask you to identify the type of conflict, choose the first action (usually: move it to a private place, stay calm, listen, focus on the client), pick the best conflict style for a scenario, or recognize behaviors that are incivility. Client safety remains the tiebreaker: when safety is at stake, the nurse stands firm.

keyTerms.def: Disagreement or discord among individuals, groups, or organizations that prevents problem solving and interferes with effective communication; normal and inevitable, never completely eliminated, but manageable constructively.

Stress or tension within one individual from real or perceived pressure caused by incompatible expectations, role conflict, or confusion (e.g., choosing between a day-shift job that interferes with family and staying on fatiguing nights).

Conflict between two or more individuals arising from differences in goals or personalities, competition, or concern about territory, control, or loss (e.g., misunderstanding a coworker’s role, belittling, or bullying).
Conflict between teams or groups in competition or opposition, often over rewards or scarce resources or scope control (e.g., physicians vs. nurse practitioners over which board regulates NPs).
Competition between two organizations in the same market (e.g., competing hospitals advertising superior care, or nursing colleges competing for applicants).
Open, visible disagreement between people or groups; because it is apparent, it can be addressed more easily and resolution can be planned.

Hidden or underlying conflict expressed through reactive or avoidant behaviors (complaining, gossiping, passive-aggression) or repressive behaviors (absenteeism, tardiness); people perceive it differently, causing stress, distress, and confusion.
The ability to manage conflict differently depending on the situation; a skill developed through ongoing practice and self-awareness (Thomas & Kilmann, 1974).
Five modes defined by assertiveness and cooperativeness: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, and accommodating.
Harsh words, threats, or generalized condemnation; it escalates conflict and should be replaced with specific, private, respectful feedback.
Rude, discourteous, or disrespectful workplace speech or behavior that violates norms of mutual respect and harms team communication and client safety.
Words, tone, or manner that humiliate, degrade, intimidate, or attack another person’s dignity.
Hostile, aggressive, harmful behavior by a nurse or group of nurses toward a coworker or peer of equal professional standing.
Repeated, health-harming mistreatment of one or more persons by one or more perpetrators through verbal abuse, offensive conduct, intimidation, or sabotage that interferes with work.
An aviation-derived team-training approach that, like TeamSTEPPS, promotes nondisciplinary problem solving and reduces barriers to speaking up.

sections.heading: Conflict is normal: where it happens and its four levels
sections.body:
Conflict can arise between clients or families and nurses, between nurses and other team members, within a unit, across a whole organization, or between an organization and its community. It interferes with problem solving and communication, and that is exactly why it threatens safety. But handled well, it is also an impetus for growth: the disagreement between a nurse and a PT about early ambulation can produce a better mobility protocol than either would have written alone.

The course adds an important nuance about avoidance. Sustained avoidance leads to negative outcomes because the problem festers. Temporary avoidance, however, can be effective when emotions are flaring—stepping away lets people regain composure before addressing the root issue. On an exam, “walk away and never bring it up” is wrong; “agree to talk after the code when both are calmer” can be right.

Classifying the level tells you who needs to be involved in solving it. Intrapersonal conflict lives inside one person and needs self-reflection, support, and sometimes a conversation with a manager about role expectations. Interpersonal conflict involves two or more people and is solved by those people, with mediation if needed. Intergroup conflict involves whole teams, so leaders and system solutions (shared protocols, resource allocation) are needed. Interorganizational conflict happens between organizations in the same market and is mostly managed at the leadership and policy level.
sections.analogy: Conflict is like a smoke alarm. The goal is not to rip the alarm off the wall so it never beeps; it is to respond early, find the source, and fix it before there is a fire. Covert conflict is the alarm with the battery removed—quiet, but the smoke is still there.

rows: A nurse torn between accepting a day shift that conflicts with child care and staying on exhausting nights
Two nurses clash over who should take a new admission; one belittles the other
ED and ICU staff disagree about when boarding clients become ICU responsibility; physicians vs. NPs over regulation
Two hospitals in the same city compete with ads for cardiac clients; nursing schools compete for applicants

check.q: The pharmacy department and the nursing department disagree over who is responsible for checking infusion pump libraries. Which level of conflict is this?
check.a: Intergroup—two groups within the organization in opposition over responsibility and resources.

sections.heading: Overt vs. covert conflict
sections.body: Overt conflict is out in the open: two people disagree in a meeting, a family member says plainly, “I am unhappy with my mother’s care.” Because everyone can see it, it is easier to address. Covert conflict hides beneath the surface. It shows up as reactive or avoidant behaviors (complaining, gossiping, passive-aggressive comments) or repressive behaviors (absenteeism, tardiness). People perceive covert conflict differently, so it generates more stress and confusion. A nurse manager who notices rising sick calls, late arrivals, and break-room whispering after an unpopular schedule change should recognize covert conflict and bring it into the open in a safe, respectful way.

rows: Recognize the pattern; surface it in a safe, nonpunitive forum

check.q: After a new charting system is introduced, several nurses begin arriving late and make sarcastic comments about “management’s brilliant idea.” Nobody has formally complained. What type of conflict is present?
check.a: Covert conflict—expressed through tardiness and passive-aggressive comments rather than open disagreement.

sections.heading: Why conflict happens: sources and triggers
sections.body: Kim et al. (2017) group sources into three layers, plus triggers specific to each type of relationship. Identifying the source points to the fix: an individual communication-style mismatch calls for self-awareness and skill-building, whereas role ambiguity calls for leaders to define role expectations.

rows: Personal characteristics, communication style, personal conflict methods
Self-inventory (Thomas–Kilmann instrument, emotional intelligence inventory), coaching
Incivility, low support, poor communication, educational differences, generational characteristics
Respectful communication norms, team training, mentoring
Role ambiguity, scope-of-practice issues, structure and workflow, work environment, resource constraints
Clear role definitions, fair workload allocation, system redesign
Lack of confidence in the nurse, need to “save face” after mistakes, preserving a patriarchal relationship
Structured communication (SBAR), nonpunitive culture, interprofessional education
Lack of knowledge, poor coping, fear and anxiety expressed as frustration, nurse failure to assess or meet needs
Assess needs, explain, involve them in decisions to restore control
Coworker disputes that, unmanaged, escalate to bullying or incivility

check.q: Two nurses argue weekly over who is supposed to restock the code cart because no one has ever been assigned the task. Which source of conflict is this, and what fix fits?
check.a: Organizational—role ambiguity and workflow. The fix is a leadership/system one: define who owns the task (role expectations), not just coaching the two nurses to get along.

sections.heading: Preventing conflict and reducing stress
sections.body:
Prevention starts with noticing early cues: rising tension or anxiety, arguments, a coworker being excluded, acting out, and snide remarks. At the staff level, the nurse addresses issues as they arise rather than letting them build; avoids destructive criticism; speaks respectfully, does not argue, and stays calm; moves the conversation to a private place away from client care areas; and listens actively, trying to see the situation from the other person’s perspective.

Nursing leaders prevent conflict by allocating resources and workloads fairly, defining role expectations clearly, inviting feedback and concerns without fear of punitive action, and acknowledging team accomplishments and significant life events. Integrative health strategies—knowing your triggers and using meditation, guided imagery, progressive relaxation, mindfulness, and self-compassion training—reduce perceived stress, increase compassion, and improve the quality of client care.
bullets: Early cues: tension, arguments, exclusion, acting out, snide remarks.
Staff: address early, no destructive criticism, calm and respectful, private place, active listening, perspective-taking.
Leaders: fair workloads and resources, clear roles, nonpunitive feedback channels, recognition of accomplishments and life events.
Self-care: know triggers; meditation, guided imagery, progressive relaxation, mindfulness, self-compassion.

check.q: A charge nurse notices that one nurse is repeatedly left out of lunch breaks and that two others make snide comments when she asks for help. What is the best early action?
check.a: Recognize these as early cues of conflict and possible incivility and address them promptly and privately—speaking with the staff involved and involving the manager if the pattern continues—rather than waiting for it to escalate.

sections.heading: Thomas–Kilmann conflict styles: picking the right tool
sections.body:
Thomas and Kilmann describe five styles on two dimensions: assertiveness (how much you pursue your own concerns) and cooperativeness (how much you try to satisfy the other person’s). No style is always right. Conflict competence is the ability to choose the style the situation needs—which requires practice and self-awareness. Most people have a default style; knowing yours helps you shift from reacting to reflecting.

NCLEX reasoning: client safety justifies competing; complex issues where both the relationship and the outcome matter call for collaborating; time pressure with equal power suits compromising; trivial issues, a need for more information, or hot emotions make avoiding acceptable short-term; and low investment on your side makes accommodating reasonable. Never accommodate or compromise on safety.

rows: Defending a critical position for client safety
Overuse appears self-centered and damages relationships
Refusing to give a medication dose that is 10 times the usual dose
Complex clinical or team issues where both relationship and outcome are critical
Nurse and PT jointly design an ambulation schedule that fits pain-med peaks and therapy times
Timely middle-ground solution when both sides have equal power
Both are only partly satisfied; never compromise on safety
Two nurses split an unpopular holiday shift in halves
Need more information, emotions need cooling, issue is trivial
Agreeing to discuss a disagreement after the code, when both are calmer
One person is much less invested than the other
Swapping break times with a coworker who needs to take a call about her child

check.q: A provider wants a nurse to give a sedative to a client whose respirations are 8/min, and suggests “half the dose” as a middle ground. Which style should the nurse use?
check.a: Competing—standing firm to hold the medication and seeking further evaluation, because client safety is at stake. Compromising (half a dose) is inappropriate when safety is at risk.

sections.heading: Responding to and managing conflict
sections.body:
When conflict is active, use a consistent approach. Be honest, trustworthy, and respectful; state the issue objectively with facts. Keep discussion from becoming emotion-based; hear all viewpoints without judging, let each person speak without interruption, and use active listening. Focus on solutions rather than blame, with safe, effective client care as the central concern. Use team-centered “we” language (“How can we solve the delay in admissions?”) rather than status-based “you” commands (“You need to take the next admission”).

Organizations support this by implementing TeamSTEPPS and Crew Resource Management, which promote nondisciplinary problem solving and lower barriers to speaking up. Individuals can use self-inventory tools such as the Thomas–Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument and an Emotional Intelligence Inventory.

With clients and families, remember that people who are sick or injured are often scared and feel a loss of control. Anger at the nurse is frequently fear in disguise. Acknowledge the emotion, gather the facts, and involve them in decisions—restoring some control de-escalates tension.
steps: Ensure safety and privacy: move the discussion away from clients and public areas; if anyone is at risk of harm, call security per policy.
Calm the temperature: stay calm, speak respectfully, and use temporary avoidance only to let emotions settle.
Let each person state the issue without interruption; listen actively and summarize what you heard.
State the issue objectively with facts, not personalities.
Use “we” language to generate solutions with client care at the center.
Agree on a plan, who does what, and when you will check back; escalate to leadership if unresolved.
sections.example: A daughter shouts at the nurse that her father’s call light has been ignored. The nurse says, “You’re worried about your dad—I want to understand what happened. Let’s step into the family room.” The nurse listens, acknowledges the delay, checks the client, and asks, “What would help him feel safer tonight? We could set hourly rounding and I can show you how the call system works.” The family regains a sense of control.

sections.heading: Incivility, verbal abuse, horizontal violence, and bullying
sections.body:
Outcome 37.6 asks you to describe the effects of incivility. Incivility is rude or disrespectful behavior—eye-rolling, sarcasm, ignoring questions, public criticism. Verbal abuse attacks dignity through words or tone. Horizontal (lateral) violence is hostility between peers of equal standing, the classic “nurses eat their young.” Workplace bullying is repeated, health-harming mistreatment, including sabotage such as withholding information needed to do the job.

These behaviors are not just unpleasant; they damage team communication and client safety. Targets stop asking questions, hesitate to call for help, and leave the profession. Unchecked nurse–nurse disputes escalate into bullying. The nurse’s response: do not participate or normalize it, address it early and directly when safe, document specific incidents (dates, behaviors, effects on care), and report through the chain of command and organizational policy. Leaders must enforce a zero-tolerance code of conduct.

rows: Rolling eyes and sighing when a new nurse asks a question
Yelling, “Are you stupid?” at the nurses’ station
A group of senior nurses excludes and undermines a peer
Isolation; the target loses help during emergencies
Repeatedly assigning the heaviest load and withholding key report information from one nurse
Missing information leads directly to client harm
Private, specific feedback about a missed assessment

check.q: A nurse repeatedly gives one coworker the heaviest assignment and leaves out key details in her handoffs. A second nurse once snapped at a coworker during a stressful code and apologized afterward. Which is workplace bullying, and why?
check.a: The first. Bullying is repeated, health-harming mistreatment that can include sabotage such as withholding information. A single incident followed by an apology is incivility to address, but it is not a repeated pattern.

sections.heading: Common traps & look-alikes

rows: Collaborating seeks a win–win that fully meets both concerns; compromising has each side give something up
Avoiding sidesteps the issue; accommodating yields to the other person’s wishes
Competing is assertive defense of a position, often for safety; bullying is repeated mistreatment of a person
Focus on the issue vs. attack on the person
Intergroup = groups within or across professions; interorganizational = separate organizations in one market
Intrapersonal is inside one person; interpersonal is between people
One nurse’s internal dilemma vs. two nurses clashing
Temporary avoidance cools emotions before addressing the issue; sustained avoidance lets conflict fester
Incivility is rude and degrading; feedback is specific, private, respectful, and aimed at improvement

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: conflict styles and first actions
sections.body:
Expect items that ask which style is being used or is most appropriate, which conflict type a scenario shows, what the charge nurse should do first when staff argue, how to respond to an angry family, and which statement by a new nurse needs further teaching. Clues: the setting (public vs. private), the stakes (safety vs. preference), the time pressure, and the relative power and investment of each party.

Sample question: Two staff nurses begin arguing loudly at the nurses’ station about who will take a new admission, within earshot of clients and visitors. Which action should the charge nurse take first? A. Assign the admission to the nurse with the lighter load. B. Ask both nurses to step into the conference room to discuss it. C. Tell both nurses that the argument will be reported to the manager. D. Ignore the argument and allow the nurses to resolve it themselves.
steps: Read the stem: loud, public interpersonal conflict near clients—privacy and the care environment are affected.
Identify what is asked: the FIRST action of the charge nurse.
Spot cues: “loudly” and “within earshot of clients and visitors.” The first problem is location and escalation.

Eliminate A: deciding may be needed later, but doing it at the station skips hearing both views and leaves the public scene unresolved. Eliminate C: a threat is destructive criticism and escalates. Eliminate D: sustained avoidance lets it fester and leaves clients exposed.
Choose B: move the discussion to a private place away from client care, then hear each side and solve the assignment issue.

Reusable strategy: for conflict-in-progress items, first secure safety and privacy and calm the situation; then listen to all parties; then solve. Threats, public decisions, and ignoring are distractors.

sections.heading: Worked case: a new nurse, a preceptor, and a near miss
sections.body: Kayla, a new graduate in week 6 of orientation, tells the charge nurse that her preceptor sighs and rolls her eyes whenever she asks a question, has called her “useless” in front of a client, and yesterday left out of report that a client was on fluid restriction. Kayla gave the client a large pitcher of water; another nurse caught it. Kayla says she is thinking of quitting and asks the charge nurse not to “make it a big deal.” The preceptor is well-liked and has worked on the unit for 15 years.
steps: Recognize cues: repeated eye-rolling and public humiliation (incivility and verbal abuse), withholding report information (sabotage), a pattern over weeks (bullying), and a near miss—client safety is now involved.
Analyze: this is interpersonal conflict that has escalated to workplace bullying; the power imbalance (preceptor vs. orientee) makes it harder for Kayla to address alone.
Prioritize: client safety and Kayla’s ability to practice safely outrank keeping it quiet. The charge nurse validates Kayla’s experience and explains why it must be addressed.

Generate solutions: document specific incidents (dates, words, effect on care); report the near miss through the safety reporting system; notify the nurse manager per policy; arrange a temporary alternate preceptor.

Take action: the manager meets privately with the preceptor, states the facts objectively, focuses on safe care and expected conduct, and sets a plan; a facilitated conversation may follow if Kayla agrees.
Evaluate: Kayla reports feeling safe to ask questions, handoffs include complete information, and no further incidents occur; the unit reviews its civility code and handoff tool.

check.q: Why isn’t “Talk to her yourself and try to get along” the best response here, even though addressing conflict directly is usually encouraged?
check.a: The behavior is repeated, involves a power imbalance, and has already affected client safety. Direct peer conversation alone is insufficient; leadership involvement and safety reporting are required.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
The NC Board of Nursing uses a Just Culture–based Complaint Evaluation Tool for practice events that distinguishes human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior. This supports the course message that organizations should use nondisciplinary problem solving (TeamSTEPPS, CRM) and encourage staff to raise concerns without fear of punitive action. A near miss caused by an incomplete handoff is reported and used to fix the system; it is not a reason to hide the event.

Not everything is a unit-level conflict, though. Conduct issues—drug diversion, impairment on duty, fraud, boundary or sexual misconduct, and confidentiality breaches—are reported to the NCBON rather than handled only by the employer. NCBON offers alternative-to-discipline programs for nurses with substance use disorders. If a conflict reveals a colleague who appears impaired on duty, the priority is client safety (remove the nurse from care per policy and notify the supervisor), followed by reporting through the proper channels.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body:
Source: Module 37 study guide, pp. 2559–2562 (conflict definition, levels, overt/covert, causes, prevention, Table 37.2 Thomas–Kilmann styles, management guidelines, conflict with clients and families, conflict competence) and the module outline p. 2563 (incivility, verbal abuse, horizontal violence, workplace bullying; Outcome 37.6).

Clarifications: (1) The source describes compromising as addressing the issue “though at the very least.” In Thomas–Kilmann terms, compromising is intermediate in both assertiveness and cooperativeness: it addresses the issue more directly than avoiding but explores it less deeply than collaborating. (2) The assertiveness/cooperativeness ratings for each style (competing high/low, collaborating high/high, avoiding low/low, accommodating low/high) were added from the Thomas–Kilmann model. (3) Collaborating takes time and is not the right choice in an emergency, where a clear directive approach is needed. (4) Incivility terms are previewed from p. 2563; the response steps (document, report via chain of command and policy, zero-tolerance codes) reflect current professional guidance (for example, ANA’s position on incivility, bullying, and workplace violence).

mnemonics.name: Who wins? (Thomas–Kilmann)
mnemonics.text: Competing = Me; Accommodating = You; Avoiding = Nobody (for now); Compromising = Half each; Collaborating = Both, fully.

mnemonics.name: PAUSE for conflict in progress
mnemonics.text: Private place, Allow each to speak, Use facts not feelings, Solutions with “we,” Evaluate and follow up.

pearls: Conflict can never be eliminated—only managed; a unit with “no conflict” may be hiding covert conflict.
Move heated discussions to a private place away from client care areas before trying to solve them.
Competing is appropriate when defending client safety; never compromise or accommodate on safety.
Temporary avoidance is acceptable to cool emotions; sustained avoidance makes conflict worse.
Gossip, sarcasm, absenteeism, and tardiness are signs of covert conflict.
Angry clients and families are often frightened and feel loss of control—involve them in decisions.
Bullying is repeated and health-harming; when it affects client safety, document and report through the chain of command.
redFlags: Information withheld during handoff as part of a personal conflict—an immediate client-safety risk.
Arguments or belittling in front of clients and families.
A new nurse who stops asking questions after repeated public criticism.
A family member’s escalating anger with threats—ensure safety and call security per policy.
A colleague who appears impaired on duty—remove from client care per policy and notify the supervisor.
recap: Conflict = disagreement that blocks problem solving and communication; normal, inevitable, manageable.
Levels: intrapersonal (within one), interpersonal (between people), intergroup (between groups), interorganizational (between organizations).
Overt conflict is open and easier to fix; covert conflict hides in gossip, passive-aggression, absenteeism, and tardiness.
Sources are individual, interpersonal, and organizational, with specific nurse–physician, nurse–client/family, and nurse–nurse triggers.
Prevent conflict by addressing issues early, privately, calmly, and with active listening; leaders allocate fairly, clarify roles, and invite nonpunitive feedback.

Thomas–Kilmann: competing for safety, collaborating for complex high-stakes issues, compromising for timely middle ground, avoiding for cooling or trivial issues, accommodating when one side cares much less.
Manage conflict with facts, no interruptions, “we” language, and client care at the center; restore control to frightened clients and families.
Incivility, verbal abuse, horizontal violence, and bullying harm communication and safety and must be reported, not normalized.

checks.q: A nurse manager notices gossip and rising sick calls after the unit changed its self-scheduling policy. What type of conflict is this, and what is the best first step?
checks.a: Covert conflict. Surface it in a safe, nonpunitive forum—such as a staff meeting or individual conversations—inviting honest feedback about the policy.

checks.q: A nurse and a physician disagree about the timing of a client’s discharge teaching; both care deeply about the outcome and the working relationship, and there is time to talk. Which style fits?
checks.a: Collaborating—a complex issue where both the outcome and the relationship matter, with time available for a win–win solution.

checks.q: A colleague wants to switch weekend shifts; the nurse has no plans and does not mind either way. Which style is reasonable?
checks.a: Accommodating—the nurse is much less invested than the colleague.

checks.q: During a code, a nurse and an RT start disagreeing about who should be documenting the events. What should they do?
checks.a: Defer the debate (temporary avoidance) but not the documentation: the code leader assigns a recorder, or one of them takes the role immediately, so the record is complete. They settle the underlying role question afterward, when both are calm, and may suggest the unit clarify code roles.

checks.q: A nurse says to a new graduate in front of a client, “Didn’t they teach you anything in school?” What is this, and what should a witnessing nurse do?
checks.a: Incivility/verbal abuse. Do not join in; support the new nurse, address the behavior privately or report it according to policy, and make sure client care is not affected.

checks.q: A family member yells that “nobody tells us anything.” Which response best de-escalates?
checks.a: Acknowledge the emotion, move to a private area, listen, and involve the family in the plan—for example, “You’re frustrated because you haven’t been updated. Let’s sit down, and I’ll go over today’s plan and what you’d like to be involved in.”
